html:
The Treaty of Point Elliott was signed on 22 January 1855 at Point Elliott, now Mukilteo, in Washington Territory, between the United States and the Coast Salish peoples of the eastern shore of Puget Sound. Governor Isaac Stevens made it as one of a series of treaties in 1854 and 1855 to open land to American settlers.

The tribes gave up their land from about Seattle north to the Canadian border and kept small reservations: Tulalip, Swinomish, Lummi and Port Madison. In return they were promised payments and the right to fish "at all usual and accustomed grounds and stations", and to hunt and gather on open land.

The signers included Chief Seattle (Si'ahl) of the Duwamish and Suquamish, and leaders of the Snohomish, Snoqualmie, Skagit and Skykomish, among many others. Many were moved to the Tulalip reservation. Some, such as the Duwamish and the Nooksack, got no reservation of their own and waited a long time for federal recognition.

Anger over the treaties helped set off the Puget Sound War of 1855 to 1856. The fishing clause mattered again a century later: in the Boldt decision of 1974 a federal judge ruled that the treaty tribes were entitled to half of the catchable fish.
